theory.intro: Dividing a power by itself gives an index of $0$, and anything divided by itself is $1$, so $x^{0}=1$. Watch what the zero is written against: one pronumeral, or a whole bracket.
facts: $\frac{x^{5}}{x^{5}}=x^{5-5}=x^{0}$, and an expression divided by itself is $1$, so $x^{0}=1$.
The index applies only to what it is written against: in $5x^{0}$ only $x$ is raised to $0$, so $5x^{0}=5\times1=5$.
Brackets extend the index to everything inside them: $(5x)^{0}=1$ and $(3ab)^{0}=1$.
A term multiplied by a zero power keeps that term: $a(bc)^{0}=a\times1=a$.
A minus sign written outside is not part of the base: $-2y^{0}=-2\times1=-2$, but $(-2y)^{0}=1$.
$x^{0}=1$ for every base except $0$, so a zero power never gives an answer of $0$.
steps: Ask what the zero index is attached to — the whole bracket, or just the pronumeral it sits on.
Work out the remaining multiplication, addition or subtraction.

foundation.solution_text:
$7a^{0}$
The zero index is written against $a$ only.
$=7\times1$
$=7$

$(2v)^{0}$
The bracket means the zero index applies to the whole term.
$=1$

$(5mn)^{0}$
Everything inside the bracket is raised to the power $0$.
$=1$

$(-3p)^{0}$
The minus sign is inside the bracket, so it is part of the base.
$=1$

$7m(np)^{0}$
Only $np$ is inside the bracket, so only that part becomes $1$.
$=7m\times1$
$=7m$

foundation.question_text: Use the index law of division on $\frac{y^{7}}{y^{7}}$ to explain why $y^{0}=1$.
foundation.solution_text:
$\frac{y^{7}}{y^{7}}$
$=y^{7-7}$
$=y^{0}$
An expression divided by itself is also equal to $1$, so $y^{0}=1$.

development.solution_text:
$4n^{0}+(4n)^{0}$
In the first term the zero applies to $n$ only; in the second it applies to the whole bracket.
$=4\times1+1$
$=4+1$
$=5$

$-7a^{0}$
$=-7\times1$
$=-7$
$(-7a)^{0}$
Here the $-7$ is inside the bracket, so it is part of the base.
$=1$

Simplify $\frac{x^{4}\times x^{5}}{x^{9}}$, giving your answer as a basic numeral.

development.solution_text:
$-(2b)^{0}$
The minus sign is outside the bracket, so only $2b$ is raised to the power $0$.
$=-1$

$4^{0}n$
The zero index is written against the $4$ only.
$=1\times n$
$=n$

mastery.question_text: A student writes $(2bc)^{0}=2$. Explain the error and state the correct answer.
mastery.solution_text:
The brackets mean the zero index applies to everything inside, including the $2$, so nothing is left outside it.
$(2bc)^{0}$
$=1$

mastery.question_text: A student writes $4+m^{0}=4$. Explain the error and state the correct answer.
mastery.solution_text:
The student treated $m^{0}$ as $0$. A zero index gives $1$, not $0$, because $\frac{m^{n}}{m^{n}}=m^{0}$ and a term divided by itself is $1$.
$4+m^{0}$
$=4+1$
$=5$

mastery.question_text: Use index laws to show that $\frac{x^{3}\times x^{4}}{x^{7}}$ equals $1$ for every non-zero value of $x$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\frac{x^{3}\times x^{4}}{x^{7}}$
$=\frac{x^{3+4}}{x^{7}}$
$=\frac{x^{7}}{x^{7}}$
$=x^{7-7}$
$=x^{0}$
$=1$
The numerator and denominator are the same power of $x$, so as long as $x$ is not $0$ the quotient is $1$.
